cards.explanation: The answer is True. Moses says, “…do not be afraid of them; for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you.” (Deuteronomy 20:1) Horses, chariots and a bigger army, and the instruction is still don't be afraid. The reason is right there in the same verse, friends.

The answer is that the LORD their God is with them. That's the whole reason. Moses says the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, is with them. (Deuteronomy 20:1) Notice he doesn't point at the swords or the numbers. He points at who is standing beside Israel.

The answer is the priest. Moses says that when they're about to go into battle, the priest is to come forward and address the army. (Deuteronomy 20:2) The officers speak after him, starting in verse 5. And the priest's message is, “…the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (Deuteronomy 20:4)

The answer is False. The priest says, “Do not be fainthearted or afraid; do not be alarmed or terrified because of them.” (Deuteronomy 20:3) Afraid, alarmed, terrified, fainthearted. He stacks them up like he really means it, friends.

The answer is fight. The priest says, “For the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (Deuteronomy 20:4) The LORD doesn't just show up to watch. He goes with them to fight for them.

The answer is, let him return home! The officers ask, “Has any man built a new house and not dedicated it? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:5) Picture him out there with a brand new house he's never even dedicated. I think his mind is back at that front door the whole time. If he falls in battle, they say, “…another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5)

The answer is that he may die and another man dedicate it. That's the reason the officers give. They say, “Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5) The house is built, and someone else could end up enjoying the dedication of it. I think that's the kind of thing a person would want to see through himself.

The answer is married. The officers say, “Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man marry her.” (Deuteronomy 20:7) That's the third man on the list, after the house and the vineyard. Three men, three reasons to head home, and each one has something good he hasn't gotten to yet.
The answer is False. The officers say, “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:8) There's no proving yourself in these words, friends. They send him home.

The answer is so his brothers' hearts won't melt like his. The officers say, “…so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own.” (Deuteronomy 20:8) Fear can spread, and the officers want to keep it from reaching the men beside him.

The answer is commanders. The text says, “When the officers have finished addressing the army, they are to appoint commanders to lead it.” (Deuteronomy 20:9) The priest had his say, the officers had their say, and THEN somebody gets put in charge. That's a lot of talking before anybody takes the lead, and I know a thing or two about waiting around for my turn.

The answer is to make an offer of peace. Moses says, “When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace.” (Deuteronomy 20:10) Peace gets offered before any fighting starts. That's a big thing to put first, friends.

The answer is that they become forced laborers. The text says, “If they accept your offer of peace and open their gates, all the people there will become forced laborers to serve you.” (Deuteronomy 20:11) The offer of peace comes first in verse 10, and accepting it is the road that skips the siege. I think this part is heavy.

The answer is True. Moses says, “But if they refuse to make peace with you and wage war against you, lay siege to that city.” (Deuteronomy 20:12) Notice the offer of peace in verse 10 comes before this, bakers. The city that refuses it and wages war is the one that gets a siege.

The answer is True. Moses says, “This is how you are to treat all the cities that are far away from you and do not belong to the nations nearby.” (Deuteronomy 20:15) That "how" points back to the peace offer in verse 10 and what follows it. Then verse 16 turns to the cities of the nations the LORD is giving Israel as an inheritance, and that's a separate command.

The answer is so they can't teach Israel what they do for their gods. That's the reason Moses gives. He says it's “…so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 20:18) The concern is Israel being led into sin against the LORD. It's a heavy passage, and the text itself gives the reason.

The answer is False. Moses says, “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit. You must not cut them down.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) He says it twice, so he means it, friends.

The answer is eat. Moses says, “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) A tree that feeds you is worth more standing than chopped down. That's one reason I'd never chop down a tree that grows cookie dough, if I could find one.

The answer is building siege works against the city. Moses says, “But you may destroy the trees that you know do not produce fruit. Use them to build siege works against the city that is waging war against you, until it falls.” (Deuteronomy 20:20) The trees with no fruit are the ones Israel may use. The fruit trees are off limits.
